Generative AI tools excel at increasing coding speed, but pure speed without structured guardrails means we are often auto-scaling our mistakes rather than simply writing code faster. We need a paradigm shift, aligning the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution. As co-author Dave Rensin outlines in the article Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering , “Design is the new code.” The EGM framework is a metaphor for a powerful way to develop AI-assisted software quickly and safely with humans intentionally in the loop. The “Elephant” is a context-rich, long-horizon AI session that holds the end-to-end architectural vision and project memory. No code is written here; it is purely dedicated to design, intent, and capturing micro-decisions. The Elephant session is where the AI interviews you and you debate the merits of your choices. This code grew out of our team's day-to-day development work, with much of the engineering done by coding agents. Treat it as research code, not production-ready software. It may still contain bugs, and its coding style and engineering practices may be inconsistent. Review and adapt it before using it in your own environment. We have adapted it for publication, so it is not identical to our internal version or the implementation described in Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System . Some designs discussed in the article are directions for future development and are not implemented in this prototype. dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person. It is also a way of working with an agent: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. 967be99077d13f07.content_excerpt: One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence.
